subject: English
title: Vocation
hook: A boy learns that every job—big or small, famous or hidden—contributes to society and deserves respect.

characters.name: Aryan
characters.role: school boy who looks down on manual labour

characters.name: Uncle Vikram
characters.role: skilled electrician who does honest work

characters.name: Mrs. Patel
characters.role: street vendor and small business owner

slides.title: Vocation
slides.storyContext: A story about the dignity of all work and finding your life's calling.

image.alt: Vocation — Vocation

slides.title: Aryan Looks Down
slides.storyContext: Aryan is a class 5 student in Mumbai whose father is a software engineer and mother is a doctor. Aryan's dream is to become a CEO or a pilot—something 'important.' One day, the electricity goes out in Aryan's building. His mother calls an electrician, Uncle Vikram, to fix it. When Vikram arrives, Aryan is embarrassed. Vikram is covered in dust, has calloused hands, and speaks in a Marathi accent. Aryan's friends are visiting, and he does not want them to see this 'low-class' man in his home. He hides in his room and refuses to say hello.
slides.inSimpleWords: Aryan has learned to judge people by their jobs and the money they make, not by their worth.

image.alt: Aryan Looks Down — Vocation

slides.title: What Is a Vocation?

points.label: Vocation = a calling or life's work
points.text: It is the job or role you choose (or sometimes falls into) that you find meaningful. Not just any job, but YOUR job.

points.label: It is not about salary or status
points.text: A vocation can be a surgeon (high-paying), a teacher (medium-paying), or a gardener (low-paying). Meaning comes from the work itself.

points.label: Every honest work is a vocation
points.text: A carpenter, a nurse, a farmer, a shopkeeper, a cleaner—all are vocations if done with pride and skill.

slides.inSimpleWords: A vocation is work you do that helps others and makes you feel proud, no matter what you earn.

image.alt: What Is a Vocation? — Vocation

slides.title: Uncle Vikram's World
slides.storyContext: Uncle Vikram finishes the electrical work in an hour. Every wire is perfectly placed, every connection tested twice. He explains to Aryan's mother: 'The main switch was loose. It could have caused a fire.' He hands her a list of recommendations—upgrade the meter, add surge protection, check the old wiring. He does not charge extra; he does it to keep her family safe. Later, as he leaves, he tells Aryan's mother: 'I have fixed electricity in 2,000 homes in this city. Good electrical work saves lives. That is why I take pride in it.'

points.label: Skill and knowledge matter in every job
points.text: An electrician must understand circuits, safety codes, and mathematics. The job requires real expertise.

points.label: Pride in work makes it noble
points.text: Uncle Vikram does not see his work as 'low.' He sees it as essential, skilled, and life-saving.

points.label: Service is the highest calling
points.text: His reward is not money alone—it is knowing that 2,000 families sleep safely because of his work.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every skilled trade—plumbing, wiring, carpentry—requires knowledge and saves lives.

image.alt: Uncle Vikram's World — Vocation

slides.title: Society Built on Many Vocations
slides.storyContext: Aryan's mother scolds him for hiding: 'Beta, let me tell you—every morning, I wake up because the water supply works. That is the plumber's vocation. The tap works because an electrician wired it. I take the car to the hospital, which exists because construction workers built it. The doctor who assists me at the hospital studied for ten years. The nurse who comforts patients has chosen healing as her vocation. The guard at the hospital protects everyone's safety. Without ANY of these vocations, my hospital cannot run. I am not more important than any of them.'

points.label: A city needs hundreds of vocations
points.text: Doctor, engineer, teacher, plumber, electrician, guard, cook, cleaner, gardener, police, nurse, farmer—all are essential.

points.label: Remove one, and the system breaks
points.text: Imagine a city without waste workers, drivers, or shopkeepers. The doctor and engineer would have nothing to eat and nowhere to live.

points.label: Each job has dignity
points.text: Equality is not pretending all jobs are the same. It is recognizing that all jobs matter.

slides.inSimpleWords: A city works only because thousands of people do hundreds of different jobs, each essential and none shameful.

image.alt: Society Built on Many Vocations — Vocation

slides.title: Finding Your Vocation: Not Just Money
slides.storyContext: One weekend, Aryan's grandmother takes him to the market. There, he meets Mrs. Patel, who runs a vegetable and fruit stall. She has been doing this for 30 years. Her hands are rough, her stall is small, and she earns maybe 300-500 rupees a day. But her stall is spotless. She knows every customer's name and their dietary needs. 'Aryan's grandmother has high blood pressure,' Mrs. Patel tells him, 'so I keep the low-salt options ready for her. My vocation is to feed my neighbourhood well. I know the best suppliers, the freshest produce. Many restaurants buy from me because they trust my judgment.' She smiles. 'I could sell inferior fruit for more profit. But my vocation would be lost.'

points.label: Vocation is about skill and integrity
points.text: Mrs. Patel could earn more by cheating. Instead, she builds trust and pride in her work.

points.label: Relationships and meaning matter more than salary
points.text: She knows 500 neighbours. They respect her. That relationship is worth more than a higher-paying dishonest job.

points.label: Small vocations change the world
points.text: She feeds a neighbourhood healthily. That is as important as a doctor, in a quiet way.

slides.inSimpleWords: A true vocation means doing your job well, with honesty and care, not just for money.

image.alt: Finding Your Vocation: Not Just Money — Vocation

slides.title: The Caste and Class Trap
slides.storyContext: Aryan's grandmother explains: 'In India, for too many years, some jobs were considered 'low caste' or shameful—cleaning, leather work, sanitation. This was a terrible injustice. People in these jobs did essential work but were treated as untouchable. Fighting this unfairness is part of building a better India. Every person, no matter their job or family background, deserves respect.' She continues: 'Today, the law protects equal rights. But shame still exists in people's minds. You—what you think about Vikram and Mrs. Patel—that shame is the old poison. You must let it go.'

points.label: Historical injustice tied work to caste
points.text: Some jobs were deemed 'low' only because certain communities were forced to do them. This was wrong.

points.label: Modern discrimination is subtle
points.text: Today, we do not always use caste language, but we still judge people by their job, accent, or appearance.

points.label: Respect is a choice
points.text: Treating someone with dignity regardless of their job is an act of building a just society.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shame attached to jobs is an old poison. Every honest person deserves respect, full stop.

image.alt: The Caste and Class Trap — Vocation

slides.title: A Real Example: Haryana's Sanitation Workers' Strike (2017)
slides.storyContext: In 2017, sanitation workers in Faridabad, Haryana went on strike, refusing to collect garbage for a week. The city became filthy. People begged the workers to return. Within days, everyone realized: these 'low-status' workers were indispensable. They were cleaning diseases, preventing plague, and keeping the city alive. They won a wage increase and better working conditions. The point: a society's respect for its workers should match their importance, not judge them by outdated notions of caste.

example.problem: A city stops paying its sanitation workers and treats them with disrespect. What happens?
example.solution: The city drowns in garbage. Disease spreads. Everyone suffers, including the rich. This proves that sanitation is not a 'low' job—it is a critical one. A just society respects and pays its essential workers well.

slides.inSimpleWords: When workers are disrespected, they strike, and everyone learns how much they really matter.

image.alt: A Real Example: Haryana's Sanitation Workers' Strike (2017) — Vocation

slides.title: Your Challenge
slides.storyContext: You have five career options: software engineer (salary: 1,00,000 rupees/month, high status, work from home), nurse (salary: 25,000 rupees/month, medium status, help sick people), teacher (salary: 40,000 rupees/month, medium status, shape young minds), factory worker (salary: 15,000 rupees/month, low status, make goods), artist (salary: varies, low status unless famous, create beauty and culture). Which would you choose as your vocation, and why?

example.problem: How do you choose a vocation if salary, status, and meaning pull in different directions?
example.solution: Ask: What problem do I want to solve? Whose life do I want to touch? What skill do I have or want to develop? What can I be proud of when I am old? If the answers point to nursing, be a nurse, even if the salary is low. You will have more meaning than a software engineer who hates their job.

slides.inSimpleWords: The best vocation is one that matches your skills, your values, and the world's needs—not just money and status.

image.alt: Your Challenge — Vocation

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: A vocation is work that is meaningful, skilled, and useful to society.
Every honest trade—plumbing, nursing, farming, cooking, teaching—is a vocation and deserves respect.
A city or nation depends on hundreds of vocations working together.
Shame attached to jobs is an old injustice. Modern society must respect all honest work.
Choosing a vocation is not just about money—it is about meaning, skill, and the difference you want to make.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your life's work is a vocation when you do it with skill, pride, and care—and all honest work deserves respect.

image.alt: What We Learned — Vocation

subject: English
title: Glass Bangles
hook: A girl discovers that skill, tradition, and women's hands have been undervalued for centuries—and decides to change it.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: curious girl who learns about glass-bangle artisans

characters.name: Mrs. Khan
characters.role: skilled glass-bangle maker with 40 years of experience

characters.name: Priya's Mother
characters.role: educated woman who supports her daughter's learning

slides.title: Glass Bangles
slides.storyContext: A story about hidden expertise, women's labour, and the value of tradition.

image.alt: Glass Bangles — Glass Bangles

slides.title: A Trip to the Bangle Market
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother takes her to Jaipur's famous bangle market during the Hindu wedding season. Rows and rows of stalls overflow with glass bangles—red, blue, green, gold, silver, multicoloured. Priya admires a set of red bangles with tiny golden dots. 'These are beautiful! How much do they cost?' she asks. 'Fifty rupees for a set of four,' the vendor replies. Priya is shocked. 'Only fifty rupees? But they are so intricate! And so many people are buying them. Why is the price so low?' Her mother smiles. 'That is a question that will teach you something important about women's work in India.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Beautiful handmade bangles sold for just 50 rupees—but who made them, and who is paid?

image.alt: A Trip to the Bangle Market — Glass Bangles

slides.title: The Hidden Skill Behind Glass Bangles
slides.storyContext: Priya visits Mrs. Khan's small house in the bangle-making neighbourhood. Inside, Mrs. Khan sits before a charcoal stove. She heats a thin glass rod until it glows orange. Using only her hands and a metal rod, she winds the hot glass around a spinning metal mandrel, shaping it into a bangle. She twists, stretches, and shapes with incredible precision. Each bangle takes about three minutes. Her hands move with perfect rhythm—thousands of bangles shaped identically over forty years. Priya watches, amazed. 'Dadi, how did you learn this?' Mrs. Khan replies: 'My mother taught me. Her mother taught her. I have been making bangles since I was five years old.'

points.label: Glass-bangle making is a skill craft
points.text: It requires training from childhood, understanding of glass temperatures, hand steadiness, and speed. Not everyone can do it.

points.label: The skill is ancient
points.text: This craft has been passed down in families for centuries. It is a living tradition of Indian craftsmanship.

points.label: But it is treated as 'women's work'
points.text: Because women primarily make bangles, the skill is undervalued. If men did the same work, it would be called 'engineering' and paid much more.

slides.inSimpleWords: Making glass bangles is an ancient, difficult craft passed from mother to daughter for centuries.

image.alt: The Hidden Skill Behind Glass Bangles — Glass Bangles

slides.title: The Economics of Invisibility
slides.storyContext: Priya asks Mrs. Khan: 'Dadi, you make these beautiful bangles. What do you earn?' Mrs. Khan sighs. 'If I make 50 bangles a day, and each bangle is sold for 50 rupees, that is 2,500 rupees. But I do not get 2,500 rupees. The middleman—the person who collects bangles from many makers like me and sells them to shops—takes a cut. Then the shop takes a cut. I receive maybe 250-300 rupees a day for my work. Sometimes only 200 rupees. And this is without any holiday, sickness, or time for my own life. My hands hurt after 12 hours of heat and repetitive work. I have burn scars on my arms and hands. But the customer pays 50 rupees for four bangles and thinks it is fair.'

points.label: Middlemen exploit artisans
points.text: The person actually making the product earns only 10% of the final price. Multiple middlemen take cuts before the customer pays.

points.label: Hidden costs are not counted
points.text: Burns, hand injuries, eye strain from the heat, back pain—these health costs are not paid by anyone. The artisan bears them.

points.label: Women's labour is traditionally undervalued
points.text: Because the work is done by women and seen as 'traditional' or 'domestic,' it is paid far less than factory work or other skilled labour.

slides.inSimpleWords: A bangle costs 50 rupees in the shop, but the woman who made it gets only 5 rupees, while middlemen and shops take the rest.

image.alt: The Economics of Invisibility — Glass Bangles

slides.title: The Tradition and the Trap
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Khan's daughter, Zainab, refused to learn bangle-making. 'I want to be a nurse,' she said. Mrs. Khan was proud but also sad. 'The tradition ends with me. No one in the next generation wants to make bangles. Who will keep the craft alive?' Priya realizes: the craft is not dying because it is not valuable. It is dying because the people who make it are so poorly paid that their own children escape it as soon as they can. 'If bangle-makers were paid like other skilled workers—like electricians or plumbers—young girls would choose to learn it,' Priya thinks. 'But because they are poor, the tradition disappears, and the world loses something beautiful.'

points.label: Tradition is alive only if the people doing it can survive
points.text: A craft dies not because it is old, but because the next generation has no economic reason to learn it.

points.label: Women escape invisible labour
points.text: When girls can study and get 'respectable' jobs, they leave traditional crafts behind. This is progress in some ways, but it loses knowledge.

points.label: The trap is economic, not cultural
points.text: If bangle-makers were paid fairly, many would choose to continue the craft and pass it to their children.

slides.inSimpleWords: A beautiful tradition dies when the people doing it are paid so little their own children refuse to learn it.

image.alt: The Tradition and the Trap — Glass Bangles

slides.title: Why Bangles Became 'Low-Value' Work
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother explains: 'Bangles have been made by Muslim artisans (mainly in Firozabad, Uttar Pradesh) and Hindu women in many regions for centuries. But when factory-made bangles arrived in the 1960s, the market changed. Factories could produce cheap bangles in bulk, undercutting handmade ones. To compete, handmade bangle-makers dropped their prices. They could not meet the demand alone, so the supply chain fragmented into many small workers and middlemen. This made it impossible for any single person to earn well. Today, the work is seen as poor and desperate, not skilled and valued.'

points.label: Industrialization often hurts traditional crafts
points.text: Factories produce faster and cheaper, but they destroy the livelihoods of skilled artisans unless those artisans can compete or shift.

points.label: Fragmentation creates exploitation
points.text: When work is broken into many small pieces and many workers, no single worker has power to demand fair wages.

points.label: Craft is devalued, not craftspeople
points.text: The skill has not decreased, but market forces and middlemen have reduced its value. This is an economic problem, not a skill problem.

slides.inSimpleWords: When factories mass-produce bangles, handmade ones have to cut prices so much that the makers become poor.

image.alt: Why Bangles Became 'Low-Value' Work — Glass Bangles

slides.title: Fair Trade: A Path Forward
slides.storyContext: Priya's mother tells her about fair-trade organisations. 'Some groups work to connect artisans directly to customers. They skip middlemen. A bangle that cost 50 rupees to a customer might now earn the maker 30 rupees instead of 5 rupees. The customer pays 100 rupees instead of 50 rupees, but the extra money goes to the person who actually made it.' Priya asks: 'Why would customers pay more?' The answer: 'Because they know the story. They know that a real woman's labour is behind the bangle. They know their money helps her send her children to school. It becomes meaningful to them—not just a cheap bangle, but a connection to someone's life.'

points.label: Fair trade connects makers and buyers directly
points.text: Removing middlemen can multiply a maker's income by 5-10 times.

points.label: Story adds value
points.text: When customers know the maker's name and story, they are willing to pay more. The bangle becomes not just a product but a connection.

points.label: Ethical consumption is possible
points.text: Customers have the power to support fair-trade artisans. Choosing handmade and fair-traded means your money reaches the maker.

slides.inSimpleWords: If customers skip middlemen and buy directly from makers, and pay fair prices, artisans can earn a living wage.

image.alt: Fair Trade: A Path Forward — Glass Bangles

slides.title: A Real Example: The Jaipur Rugs Foundation
slides.storyContext: In Rajasthan, the Jaipur Rugs Foundation connects artisan rug weavers directly to international buyers. Weavers who used to earn 50 rupees per day now earn 200-300 rupees daily. They have healthcare, their children attend school, and they are training the next generation in the craft. By cutting out middlemen and ensuring fair wages, a 500-year-old craft has been saved and is now thriving. Weavers are proud of their work again.

example.problem: Traditional crafts are dying because artisans are too poor to survive. How do you save the craft and respect the craftspeople?
example.solution: Fair-trade models, direct-to-customer sales, government support, craft museums, and education programs can all help. When artisans earn dignified wages, they stay in the craft, teach the next generation, and preserve knowledge that is irreplaceable.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fair-trade movements prove that artisans can earn dignity and tradition can survive when they are paid justly.

image.alt: A Real Example: The Jaipur Rugs Foundation — Glass Bangles

slides.title: Your Challenge
slides.storyContext: You want to buy bangles for your mother's birthday. You can either: (1) Buy cheap factory bangles from the mall for 50 rupees per set, or (2) Buy handmade fair-trade bangles online for 150 rupees per set, knowing the maker's name and story. You have limited money. What do you choose, and why? How would you explain your choice to your mother?

example.problem: Handmade bangles cost three times more than factory-made ones. Is it worth paying extra?
example.solution: If you care about: (a) the artisan's survival and fair wages, (b) the preservation of tradition and craft, (c) meaningful gifts with stories, then yes, pay extra. If you care only about price, buy cheap. But understand the cost of cheap: someone is being underpaid for their skill and labour.

slides.inSimpleWords: Choosing fair-trade means paying more but ensuring the maker gets paid what their skill deserves.

image.alt: Your Challenge — Glass Bangles

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Glass-bangle making is an ancient, skilled craft passed down through generations.
But bangle-makers are paid extremely poorly—sometimes only 10% of what the customer pays.
Women's traditional labour has been historically undervalued in India and worldwide.
Middlemen and factory competition have driven down prices so much that artisans cannot survive.
Fair trade, direct sales, and customer awareness can help restore dignity and fair wages to artisans.

slides.inSimpleWords: Handmade bangles are beautiful and skilled, but the makers have been underpaid for centuries. Fair trade is changing that.

image.alt: What We Learned — Glass Bangles

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It
title: Arjun's Money Mystery
hook: Why does a shopkeeper accept coins and notes? Let's find out!

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: curious student who loves the market

characters.name: Dadaji
characters.role: wise grandfather who teaches about money

characters.name: Mrs. Sharma
characters.role: vegetable vendor at the local market

slides.title: Arjun's Money Mystery
slides.storyContext: Arjun discovers why money works.

image.alt: Arjun's Money Mystery — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: The Market Adventure
slides.storyContext: One Sunday morning, Arjun goes to the market with Dadaji to buy vegetables. Mrs. Sharma, the vegetable vendor, gives them fresh tomatoes and spinach. Arjun gives her some coins and notes. Mrs. Sharma smiles and says, 'This is called money—a magical thing that makes trading easy!' Arjun is curious: Why is money magic? Why can't we just swap things?

image.alt: The Market Adventure — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: What is Money?
slides.storyContext: Dadaji explains: Before money, people traded things directly (barter). Arjun's great-great-grandpa might have traded rice for cloth. But that was very hard! What if the cloth seller didn't want rice?

points.text: Money is something everyone agrees has value and accepts in exchange for goods.
It solves the barter problem—everyone accepts money, so you can trade easily.

slides.inSimpleWords: Money is like a magic ticket—everyone wants it, so you can trade it for anything you need.

image.alt: What is Money? — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: Coins: Small but Mighty
slides.storyContext: Arjun touches the coins in his pocket—a shiny ₹1 coin, two ₹5 coins, and a ₹10 coin. Mrs. Sharma says, 'These coins are made of metal and last a very long time.'

points.text: Coins are round, flat metal money with a value stamped on them.
In India, common coins are ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, and ₹10.
Coins are hard to damage and last for many years.

example.problem: Arjun has 3 coins of ₹5 each. How much money does he have?

slides.inSimpleWords: Coins are small pieces of metal worth different amounts—like ₹5, ₹10—and they stay in good shape for years.

image.alt: Coins: Small but Mighty — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: Notes: Bigger Value, Lighter Weight
slides.storyContext: Dadaji pulls out a ₹100 note from his wallet. Arjun is amazed: 'Wow! This thin paper is worth 100 coins?' Dadaji laughs, 'Yes, and much lighter to carry!'

points.text: Notes are paper money printed by the government (Reserve Bank of India makes them).
Each note has a number (the denomination) and is unique to prevent counterfeiting.

example.problem: Dadaji has one ₹100 note and one ₹50 note. How much does he have altogether?

slides.inSimpleWords: Notes are like colored paper money made by the government—they're lighter than coins but worth much more.

image.alt: Notes: Bigger Value, Lighter Weight — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: Why We Use Money Instead of Barter
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks Dadaji, 'Grandfather, why can't we just trade vegetables for cloth like in the old days?' Dadaji smiles and explains with three real problems.

points.label: Problem 1: Double Coincidence
points.text: In barter, the seller must want EXACTLY what the buyer has. Mrs. Sharma sells vegetables but maybe wants cloth. If the cloth seller wants rice (not vegetables), they can't trade!

points.label: Problem 2: Hard to Divide
points.text: If a cow costs 10 chickens, but you only need to trade 7 chickens—you can't cut a chicken! Money divides easily: ₹100 = 2 × ₹50.

points.label: Problem 3: Hard to Store
points.text: You can't store 100 chickens for a year (they spoil or die). But 100 rupees stay in your pocket forever!

slides.inSimpleWords: Money makes trade fair and simple—anyone will take it, it divides easily, and it doesn't spoil.

image.alt: Why We Use Money Instead of Barter — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: The Two Kinds of Money in Your Pocket
slides.storyContext: At the end of their market trip, Arjun counts his money: coins and notes mixed together. He realizes both are money, but they're different.

points.text: Coins: metal, heavy, good for small amounts, lasts forever.
Notes: paper, light, good for bigger amounts, printed by RBI.
Together, coins + notes = the money you use every day.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coins are like small change you feel in your hand; notes are like folded paper money for bigger purchases.

image.alt: The Two Kinds of Money in Your Pocket — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: A Day at the Market (Full Example)
slides.storyContext: Arjun and Dadaji go to buy: 1 kg of tomatoes (₹30), 500g of spinach (₹20), and a loaf of bread (₹40). Dadaji gives Mrs. Sharma two ₹50 notes. How much change should they get?

image.alt: A Day at the Market (Full Example) — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: Your Turn: Money at the Shop
slides.storyContext: You go to the corner shop with ₹100 in your pocket. You buy a notebook for ₹35 and a pencil for ₹15. How much money do you have left?

example.problem: Total spent: ₹35 + ₹15 = ₹50. You started with ₹100. Money left = ?

image.alt: Your Turn: Money at the Shop — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Arjun now understands money! Let's recap.

points.text: Money is something everyone accepts in trade—it solves the barter problem.
Coins are small metal money (₹1, ₹5, ₹10 etc.); notes are paper money (₹10, ₹50, ₹100 etc.).
We use money because it's easy to divide, easy to store, and everyone wants it.
Money makes buying and selling simple and fair for everyone.

slides.inSimpleWords: Money is the tool we use to trade fairly for what we need—coins and notes together make it work.

image.alt: What We Learned — What is Money? Coins, Notes & Why We Use It
